opus-5.5.text:
Sure. So the basic idea, and GelSight is the best-known example, is that you have a soft elastomer, a clear silicone gel, with a thin reflective coating painted on the outside surface. Behind it there's a small camera and some colored LEDs lighting the gel from different angles.

When you press that gel against an object, the coating deforms and takes on the shape of whatever it's touching. From the camera's point of view, looking through the clear gel at the back of that coating, you see what looks almost like a little relief map or embossing of the surface. Because the lights come from different directions, the slopes of the deformation show up as different colors and shading. You can actually run photometric stereo on that and reconstruct a pretty detailed 3D height map of the contact.

What's striking is the resolution. You can see the ridges of a fingerprint, the texture of fabric, the printing on a coin, the threads on a screw. It's often finer than what you'd get from a regular camera looking at the object, because the object is right up against the sensor and the lighting is completely controlled.

Many of these sensors also have a pattern of little dots or markers embedded in the gel. As you push, twist, or drag the object, those markers shift, and by tracking them you can estimate shear forces and detect when something is starting to slip, which matters a lot for grasping. So you're getting geometry, contact area, and a rough sense of force and slip, all from what is basically a camera image.

The catch, and this is something I always emphasize, is that it's still a very local view. You see a small patch, the gel wears out and tears, the sensors are bulky compared to a human fingertip, and turning those images into good manipulation decisions is still hard. So it's a beautiful window into contact, but it doesn't by itself solve the dexterity problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes a relief map or embossing that follows the object’s surface, but does not clearly communicate that the view is a negative impression.

fable-5.1.text:
So picture a little block of clear, soft silicone gel, and on the back of it you've got a tiny camera looking through it. The front surface of the gel is coated with a thin reflective membrane, and there are LEDs shining in from the sides, usually in different colors from different directions.

When you press that gel against an object, the membrane deforms. It takes on the shape of whatever you're touching. And because the lighting is coming in from different angles, the camera sees that deformation as a pattern of shading, almost like a topographic map. If you press it against a bolt, you see the threads. If you press it against a coin, you can read the embossed lettering. The resolution is remarkable, far finer than what your fingertips can resolve.

What really surprised me the first time I saw it is that it looks like a photograph of the object's surface geometry. Not an image of the object in the usual sense, with color and texture, but a kind of relief image. Edges show up as bright and dark ridges. Flat regions are smooth. You can see where contact is happening and where it isn't, so you get a contact patch, and you get the shape within that patch.

And then if you put little dots or markers on the membrane, you can also watch those dots move. As the object slides or rotates, the dots shift, so you get shear and torque information too. That's the part that matters a lot for grasping, because you can detect slip before the object actually falls out of the gripper.

So the honest answer is that you see a lot. In some ways it's too much. The challenge for us in robotics hasn't been getting the signal, it's been figuring out what to do with it. A human doesn't consciously process thousands of pixels of contact geometry. We just feel that the cup is slipping and we squeeze. Getting a robot to go from that very rich image to a useful decision is still, I think, mostly an open problem.

r001.rationale: The response says the membrane deforms to take on the shape of the object and creates a relief image, but it does not describe that view as a negative impression of the object's surface.

astra-6.text: Imagine a little camera looking at the inside of a soft gel pad. When you press an object against the pad, the gel deforms around it, and the camera sees that deformation. So you get this wonderfully detailed image of the contact — the shape of an edge, the texture of a surface, even very fine ridges. You’re essentially turning touch into something you can see.

r001.rationale: The response says the gel deforms around the object and the camera sees that deformation, but it does not describe the view as a negative impression of the object's surface.

sol-6.1.text: What you see is essentially an image of the contact surface. There’s a camera looking at the underside of a soft gel, and when an object presses into it, the gel deforms around the object’s shape. So you can see very fine details—the texture, little ridges, edges—that might be difficult to pick out with an ordinary camera. It’s a way of turning touch into something we can process visually.

r001.rationale: The response says the camera shows an image of the contact surface and that the gel deforms around the object, but it does not describe the view as a negative impression of the object's surface.
